items.title: From Newsletter to Journal in an Evening: A Human–AI Workflow for Rapid, Open and Verified Publication of Applied Education Research
items.abstract: AI in education is changing faster than conventional academic publishing can follow. A paper that takes a year to reach print may describe tools, policies and evidence that have already been superseded. This article describes an experiment in doing things differently. Over a single evening in October 2026, a practitioner-scholar and an AI agent turned a body of 81 long-form newsletter articles on AI in education into ten thematic papers, each with original figures, verified references and an open disclosure of how it was made, and published them in Future Science Archives, a non-profit, open-review archive. The article sets out the motivation for the experiment, including the author's long interest in educational innovation and his concerns about the economics of academ‐ ic publishing. It describes the venue and its strengths and limitations, the source corpus, the workflow and the division of labour between human and AI, and the verification process, which found and corrected more than two dozen errors, unverifiable claims and one retracted study carried over from the newsletters. It reports the actual publication timeline. It then discusses the risks of the approach, including "research slop", weakened rigour and researchers becoming editors of machine-written text, and argues that these risks are real but manageable when the human remains responsible for judgement and the process is transparent. It closes with a replicable workflow for others.

items.title: From Posters to Prompting: Reimagining CME in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Medical education is evolving rapidly alongside the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs). Continuing medical education (CME) has traditionally relied on educational modalities sometimes conceptualized as the “three P’s” of Posters, Podium presentations, and Publications, later expanded into the “seven P’s” with the addition of Podcasts, Play, Peer-to-peer learning, and Patient interactions. This commentary proposes Prompting as an eighth “P” of CME, reflecting the growing importance of effectively interacting with AI systems in clinical and academic practice. Prompting refers to the process of crafting and refining instructions that guide AI-generated outputs. The quality, specificity, and contextual framing of prompts substantially influence the accuracy and usefulness of responses generated by LLMs. Emerging evidence suggests that prompting is a learnable skill that can improve educational and clinical utility without requiring advanced technical expertise. This commentary reviews key prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, role-based, chain-of-thought, and iterative prompting, and discusses their relevance to healthcare providers. Applications across clinical care, medical education, patient communication, administration, and research are explored. Potential benefits include generating differential diagnoses, summarizing medical literature, creating educational materials, supporting clinical simulations, and improving patient-facing communication. The commentary also addresses important risks associated with LLM use, including hallucinations, automation bias, and overreliance on AI-generated content. Ultimately, prompting is framed not only as a mechanism for learning through AI systems, but also as a modern medical literacy competency that healthcare providers must actively develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education.

items.title: Gamified Interface Design Enhances Student Engagement in Synchronous Video Conferencing Learning
items.abstract: Abstract The widespread adoption of video conferencing (VC) platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic has transformed synchronous higher education, yet sustaining student engagement in such environments remains a persistent challenge, particularly in creative disciplines. This study investigated the effectiveness of three gamification elements included animated badges, experience points, and level upgrades in enhancing behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement within a synchronous VC learning context. Guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study employed a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group design involving 124 first-year undergraduate graphic design students from three public universities in China. Participants were assigned to a non-gamified control group or one of three gamified conditions and completed pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring multidimensional engagement. Paired t-test analyses revealed statistically significant improvements across all engagement dimensions in the gamified groups (p < 0.001), while the control group exhibited minimal or no meaningful change. Experience points produced the most consistent gains across behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement, whereas level upgrades yielded the strongest effects on deep cognitive processing and metacognitive regulation. Animated badges were particularly effective in enhancing emotional engagement and learning enjoyment. One-way ANOVA results further indicated clear performance differentiation between gamified and non-gamified conditions. These findings displayed that well-designed gamification mechanisms can substantially enhance engagement in synchronous VC environments by supporting learners’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The study contributes empirical evidence to gamification and online learning literature and offers practical guidance for educators and platform designers seeking to improve motivation, interaction, and learning quality in real-time digital instruction.

items.title: Gap analysis of AI ethical guidelines in the medical sector: a comprehensive review
items.abstract: Ethical principles are essential to the responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare. This study examines the explicit lexical representation of predefined ethical themes in a selected corpus of 73 healthcare-AI publications. A nine-theme ethical codebook was developed from institutional guidance and relevant peer-reviewed literature. The study applied NLP-supported full-text analysis, inductive topic modeling, deductive codebook-guided content analysis, theme-based corpus analysis, and paper-level statistical comparison. The findings showed substantial variation in thematic representation. Fairness, accountability, and privacy received the strongest overall representation. Fairness had the highest raw keyword frequency, whereas accountability had the highest median adjusted occurrence rate. Transparency showed moderate representation and was mainly associated with explainability-related discussion. Patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact showed the weakest representation, while safety, innovation and progress, and collaboration and partnership received comparatively less attention. Friedman and Holm-adjusted pairwise analyses confirmed significant differences among themes. These findings characterize patterns of ethical-theme representation within the selected healthcare-AI literature corpus. The study proposes measurable indicators to support future healthcare-AI research, governance, and responsible system development.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI IN EFL ACADEMIC WRITING: A CRITICAL REVIEW AND IMPLICATIONS FOR HIGHER EDUCATION IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support academic writing in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. This focused narrative review critically examines selected empirical studies, research syntheses, and institutional guidance published between 2023 and 2026. It distinguishes improvements in AI-assisted texts from evidence of lasting, independent writing competence and considers feedback, critical thinking, learner autonomy, and academic integrity. The discussion incorporates emerging research from Uzbekistan while acknowledging the limited generalizability of individual institutional studies. The synthesis suggests that AI feedback can support revision when students critically evaluate suggestions, verify sources, and retain responsibility for their writing. As a conceptual contribution, the article proposes a five-stage instructional framework comprising independent planning, targeted AI assistance, critical evaluation, student-led revision, and reflection. The framework has not been empirically tested. The article concludes by identifying priorities for responsible classroom implementation and future research in Uzbek higher education.

items.title: Generative AI in Managerial Decision-Making: A Systematic Literature Review of Trust, AI Literacy, and Decision Quality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering managerial decision processes, yet evidence remains fragmented regarding when AI-generated advice should be trusted, how managers should evaluate it, and how decision quality should be assessed. This study systematically reviews GenAI-supported managerial decision-making by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening, bibliometric mapping, author-keyword co-occurrence analysis, thematic synthesis, and the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework. A Scopus export containing 3,500 records was screened using temporal, language, document-type, topical, and contextual criteria, yielding 99 studies published between 2024 and 2026. The final corpus comprises 342 unique authors across 94 publication sources. Four themes dominate: decision augmentation and analytics; trust, governance, and explainability; human–AI collaboration and capability; and decision quality and organizational outcomes. Trust is more often represented through governance, transparency, explainability, calibration, and human oversight than as an explicitly measured construct, while AI literacy appears explicitly in only one study. Decision quality is likewise rarely conceptualized directly and is commonly proxied by accuracy, efficiency, or predictive performance. The review proposes an integrative model in which GenAI decision-support capabilities influence managerial decision quality through calibrated trust and human–AI collaboration, with AI literacy functioning as a critical capability for verification and appropriate reliance. The study concludes with a TCCM-based research agenda for human-centered GenAI decision research. Keywords: generative AI; managerial decision-making; trust in AI; AI literacy; decision quality

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

items.title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
items.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

items.title: Hidden Costs of Vibe Coding: Code Quality, Technical Debt, and Security
items.abstract: This presentation examines the hidden costs and long-term implications of vibe coding, an emerging approach to software development in which artificial intelligence generates software implementations from natural-language instructions with limited human review of the resulting source code. While AI-assisted coding can significantly accelerate initial software development and reduce short-term implementation costs, it may introduce substantial challenges related to code quality, technical debt, cybersecurity, software maintainability, and developer competence. The presentation explores the productivity paradox of AI-generated software, highlighting how immediate efficiency gains may be offset by increased maintenance requirements, architectural complexity, code duplication, and difficulties in understanding and modifying generated solutions. Particular attention is devoted to the accumulation of technical debt and its potential to undermine long-term software engineering productivity. Drawing on recent empirical studies and industry reports, the presentation discusses security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, including inadequate access controls, exposure of sensitive information, and the gap between functional correctness and security compliance. It also examines the effects of AI-assisted programming on developers' learning outcomes, the unpredictability of AI service costs, and the risks of vendor lock-in. The presentation concludes by emphasizing the importance of responsible AI-assisted software development, including clear specifications, architectural guidelines, human oversight, systematic code review, rigorous testing, security verification, organizational governance, and continuous professional training.

items.title: Higher education governance under AI and geopolitical disruption: a socio-technical framework for administrative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has reached the administrative core of the universities, where students are recruited, admitted and supported. We call this administrative AI, meaning chatbots, predictive analytics and automated screening applied to administration rather than to teaching. It arrived rapidly, at an uncertain moment for higher education governance. Geopolitical upheaval is troubling student mobility and internationalisation, and universities whose finances depend on international enrolment are discovering how resilient they are. Research has been slow to follow, remaining confined to teaching and learning. Where administrative AI is noticed, it is classified as routine efficiency, far from the politics of mobility or the question of what institutions can govern. We ask three questions here. What motivates higher education institutions (HEIs) to include AI in their administrative services, and what global and geopolitical forces shape those drivers? How do such systems intersect with visa regimes, with regional education hubs, and with the financial exposure of universities that depend on international enrolment? And which governance conditions make administrative AI strengthen institutional resilience, equity and participation, and which let it erode them? Socio-technical systems theory supplies our main lens, with globalisation and diffusion research working behind it. From these perspectives we build a framework of five drivers, which are infrastructural readiness, competitive positioning under enrolment volatility, regulatory and mobility mandates, commercial platform ecosystems and sustainability legitimacy. We give each one a mechanism, a cast of actors and a characteristic risk, and different combinations direct institutions to different paths. Three socio-technical propositions organise the reading, examined against institutional cases and six documented episodes in which administrative or mobility automation failed or faced resistance. We also take up higher education as a site of soft power, automation's effect on staff as well as student mobility, and the leadership capabilities without which governance conditions stay on paper. Our central claim is that administrative AI poses a governance question rather than a merely technical one. Whether it produces resilience or dependency turns on procurement terms, contestability, who takes part, and what gets audited. The technology settles none of it.

items.abstract: Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan otomatisasi telah mengubah secara fundamental tatanan dunia kerja, pola pendidikan, dan model pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. Fenomena disrupsi ini melahirkan tuntutan baru terhadap konsep human capital, dari sekadar modal tenaga kerja fisik menuju konsep “Human Capital 5.0” yang menekankan keselarasan antara kompetensi manusia yang berpusat pada nilai-nilai kemanusiaan (human-centered) dengan kecanggihan teknologi berbasis data (technology-based). Artikel ini bertujuan mengkaji peran pendidikan dan manajemen sumber daya manusia dalam merespons disrupsi AI dan otomatisasi, serta menganalisis kontribusi ekonomi digital dan kecerdasan buatan terhadap kualitas pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Metode yang digunakan adalah studi kepustakaan (library research) dengan pendekatan deskriptif-kualitatif terhadap literatur ilmiah nasional dan internasional. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa pendidikan berperan strategis melalui reorientasi kurikulum berbasis literasi digital, penguatan pembelajaran sepanjang hayat (lifelong learning), dan pengembangan soft skill yang relatif sulit digantikan mesin; sementara manajemen sumber daya manusia berperan melalui strategi reskilling dan upskilling yang selaras dengan kebutuhan industri. Dari sisi ekonomi digital, pemanfaatan AI dan business intelligence terbukti mampu meningkatkan kecepatan, ketepatan, dan akurasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis, khususnya pada sektor Usaha Mikro, Kecil, dan Menengah (UMKM), meskipun kesenjangan akses teknologi dan literasi digital di wilayah kepulauan dan pedesaan seperti Nusa Tenggara Barat masih menjadi tantangan tersendiri. Artikel ini merekomendasikan penguatan sinergi tiga pihak (triple helix) antara lembaga pendidikan, dunia usaha, dan pemerintah daerah untuk membangun ekosistem Human Capital 5.0 yang inklusif, adaptif, dan berkelanjutan. Kata kunci: Human Capital 5.0; disrupsi kecerdasan buatan; ekonomi digital; pengambilan keputusan bisnis; pendidikan vokasi.

items.title: Human--AI Interactions as First-Class Data: A Formal Interaction Model and Runtime for Explainable AI Collaboration
items.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.

items.title: Human-Resource Digital Transformation Trends in Private Universities in India
items.abstract: The digital transformation is reshaping the functioning of academic, administrative and human-resource operations in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the implementation of digital HR in the private Universities of India, specifically on the following digital HR practices: payroll automation, employee self-service, online recruitment, digital performance appraisal, learning management systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and HR analytics. The descriptive survey design was adopted and the data were obtained from 60 HR professionals and administrative personnel in private higher education institutions. The results indicate that high adoption of payroll automation and employee self-service portals and on the other hand, AI-based recruitment and HR analytics are still in their early stages. Financial challenges, employee resistance, lack of digital skills, integration of systems and data-security issues are the main challenges identified. The results have shown that the HR automation process in private Universities is moving from simple automation to more sophisticated and data-oriented HR processes; however, sophisticated digital HR is still at its beginning stage. items.title: iLeapTutor: a RAG-enabled generative AI platform for standards-aligned university course authoring
items.abstract: Introduction Recent advances in Artificial intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled more dynamic digital learning experiences. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) leverage this capability to improve learning outcomes by offering structured and responsive support. This paper introduces iLeap Tutor , an intelligent learning platform that delivers consistent, structured, course-aligned learning materials that meet course requirements, such as Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and National E-learning Center (NeLC) standards. Methods iLeap Tutor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the tutor's uploaded course materials together with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (Preview), with prompts that embed the CLO and NeLC requirements, and the tutor reviews and approves the generated course. The platform was evaluated as a single-course proof-of-concept using the Selected Topics in Computer Science course at Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (IAU). The generated content was assessed using BERTScore, Self-BLEU, and latency measurements, and thirteen academic experts evaluated the generated course in terms of content accuracy, alignment with CLOs, structure, language quality, and platform usability. Results The evaluation achieved a BERTScore-F1 of 0.829 and a cross-run Self-BLEU result of 0.553 and a within-lesson Self-BLEU of 0.146, while the generation of 16 course topics averaged 219 s in latency. At least 92.3% of responses on every questionnaire item indicated agreement, and all of them would recommend the platform. Discussion The results indicate strong semantic alignment and output consistency across multiple runs and within-lesson content diversity.

items.title: IMPLEMENTASI GAMIFIKASI PEMBELAJARAN (GAMIFICATION) BERBASIS GAME “BLOOKET” UNTUK MENINGKATKAN PEMAHAMAN MEMBACA SISWA KELAS III SD INPRES 3/77 BOTTO PADANG
items.abstract: This study aims to improve the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang through the implementation of gamified learning using the Blooket game. The main problem underlying this research is the low level of students’ reading comprehension, characterized by difficulties in understanding texts, low learning motivation, and limited student engagement due to the use of conventional teaching methods. This research employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) approach based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles. The research subjects were 14 third-grade students of SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Data were collected through reading comprehension tests, observation sheets, motivation questionnaires, and interviews. The data were analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The results of the study indicate that the implementation of gamification through Blooket significantly improves students’ reading comprehension. This improvement is evident from the increase in students’ average reading comprehension scores from the pre-cycle to Cycle I and further improvement in Cycle II. In addition, the use of Blooket enhances students’ intrinsic motivation and engagement in reading activities. Supporting factors include attractive visual displays, point and ranking systems, and instant feedback provided by the Blooket platform. items.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
items.abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

items.title: Industry 5.0 Smart Organizations: Adopting Agentic AI for Business Optimization in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As technology continues to advance and enterprises increasingly deploy innovative digital technologies to power and transform their business processes, Smart Organizations are adopting Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) to automate, optimize, and enhance operational performance in the digital age. Unlike conventional AI systems that primarily execute predefined tasks and provide analytical insights, Agentic AI possesses autonomous decision-making, adaptive learning, goal-oriented reasoning, and proactive execution capabilities that enable organizations to respond dynamically to changing business environments. Within the context of Industry 5.0, which emphasizes human-centricity, sustainability, resilience, and intelligent collaboration between humans and machines, Agentic AI is emerging as a strategic enabler of business optimization and organizational transformation. This study explores the adoption of Agentic AI within industry 5.0 Smart Organizations and examines its impact on operational efficiency, decision-making quality, workforce productivity, customer experience, supply chain performance, and organizational resilience. Drawing upon Human–AI Collaboration Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and Industry 5.0 principles, the research proposes a conceptual framework that integrates autonomous AI agents, human expertise, and digital enterprise ecosystems to create adaptive and self-optimizing organizations. The study further investigates the critical success factors influencing Agentic AI adoption, including technological readiness, organizational culture, governance structures, workforce competencies, data infrastructure, and ethical considerations. The findings demonstrate that Agentic AI significantly contributes to business optimization by reducing operational inefficiencies, improving resource utilization, accelerating decision cycles, enhancing predictive capabilities, and enabling continuous process improvement. Furthermore, the research argues that the convergence of Industry 5.0 and Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from traditional automation toward autonomous, collaborative, and intelligent enterprise ecosystems where humans and AI agents work synergistically to generate sustainable business value. The study contributes to the emerging body of knowledge on Industry 5.0 by providing theoretical and practical insights into how Smart Organizations can strategically leverage Agentic AI to achieve competitive advantage, organizational agility, and long-term business sustainability in the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa y escritura autorregulada
items.abstract: In the context of foreign language writing, studies suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning supports knowledge acquisition and increases motivation (Chen & Gong, 2025). However, its use requires a meticulous implementation due to deficiencies in academic rigor and citation accuracy, as well as the risk of over-reliance (Chen & Gong, 2025; Solak, 2024). Through a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-intervention measures, this study evaluates the efficacy of a GenAI-mediated pedagogical sequence on argumentative writing performance. Following a process-based writing approach (Flower & Hayes, 1981), 39 second-year English Language Teaching (ELT) students participated in five sessions focused on self-assessment and draft editing. These sessions were assisted by tools such as Gemin (for IELTS rubric-based draft evaluation), Quillbot (for grammar and style correction), and Lextutor (for lexical profiling). The results confirm that GenAI —when integrated into a structured sequence— seems to strengthen L2 writing clarity, making it more precise and readable by optimizing feedback and promoting the critical, self-regulated use of these tools for essay improvement. Furthermore, the high level of student satisfaction with the resources used highlights the importance of fostering digital literacy and enhancing the role of GenAI as a pedagogical complement. This approach promotes the ethical integration of emerging technologies into writing instruction within Higher Education.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial y competencias de aprendizaje en programación
items.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education programming raises questions about its influence on learning autonomy and critical thinking. This stems from theoretical concerns about technological dependency and from the limited regional empirical evidence on how these effects vary by experience level. This quantitative study examines whether experience level (novices vs. advanced) and AI usage frequency associate with these constructs among computer science students in Costa Rica. Using a cross-sectional design, 99 students from Universidad Hispanoamericana de Costa Rica were classified as novices (n = 79) or advanced (n = 20), via the Dreyfus & Dreyfus (1986) model with 5 weighted indicators. Accordingly, autonomy (а = 0,685) and critical thinking (а = 0,742) were measured, and both constructs were analyzed using Welch t-tests, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression. Autonomy showed suggestive evidence of being higher in advanced students [t(49,2) = 2,079, p = 0,043, g = 0,386], though nonparametric analysis did not confirm this [U = 614,5, p = 0,125]. Critical thinking showed no significant difference [t(42,1) = 1,816, p = 0,077, g = 0,361], and AI usage frequency was not associated with autonomy [r = 0,166, p = 0,101] or critical thinking [r = 0,123, p = 0,226]. Both constructs showed robust correlation [r = 0,552, p < 0,001; р = 0,533, p < 0,001]. The 88,9 % active modification rate suggests students use AI as cognitive support, potentially explaining the null associations. Given that 85,9 % support regulated use and 10,1 % favor prohibition, these preliminary findings suggest that promoting ethical regulated AI use may be preferable to restriction.

items.title: Is Gen AI an editor or a revision tool? A case study of EFL students in AI-assisted revision
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools become increasingly integrated into language education, understanding how learners respond to AI-generated feedback during writing revision has become an important research concern. Existing studies have primarily examined the effects of AI on writing performance, with less attention to learners’ reported decision-making and reflection during revision. This qualitative study investigated learner-AI interaction, reported revision practices and learner perceptions among 18 first-year non-English-major students enrolled in a university EFL writing course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews following a Gen AI-assisted revision task and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings identified three interaction patterns with Gen AI: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, metacognitive AI engagement. Participants differed in how they evaluated and used AI-generated feedback, including passive acceptance, selective uptake, and critical evaluation. Some reported increased confidence, motivation, and awareness of linguistic form, whereas others expressed concerns about overreliance, authorship, and loss of personal voice. These self-reported experiences provide insight into how EFL learners perceive and manage GenAI-assisted revision, highlighting the need for pedagogical approaches that foster critical AI literacy and reflective learner autonomy.

items.title: It’s Not the Tool, It’s the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
items.abstract: Current generative AI models solve introductory physics problems at expert level. Kortemeyer (2026) reports that GPT-5 Thinking scores 27/30 on physics finals and 92.3% on a representation translation test, categorizing problems by solution method rather than surface features: a hallmark of expert cognition. As of summer 2026, most standard kinematics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism problems can be solved almost instantaneously. Small accommodations accumulate quietly: allowing AI-generated visualizations here, AI-assisted explanations there. The real danger lies not in incorrect outputs, but in the gradual erosion of students' engagement in epistemic practices: the ways of thinking, predicting, and evaluating evidence that define scientific reasoning. Kortemeyer calls this the "boiling frog problem": educational systems may adapt so incrementally to AI capabilities that their foundational learning goals are no longer questioned until it is too late to reverse course. This paper proposes a constructive, classroom-ready answer at the level of individual instructional design. It presents AIRIS as a deliberately practice-oriented condensation of a broader, more fine-grained theoretical account of how cognitive regulation is distributed in hybrid human-AI cognition. Drawing on research in self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence, AIRIS structures student work across three phases: before, during, and after AI use. The relevant question is not whether AI augments performance (it undeniably does), but whether that augmentation enhances or displaces the cognitive work essential to learning. The answer lies not in the tool, but in the task.

items.abstract: For one to achieve meaningful learning, Knowledge acquisition is a very crucial factor that should never be undermined, however, we should also note that the learner's possession of information does not necessarily mean that he understands all the concepts or is able to apply them in unfamiliar situations. This narrative literature review examines how knowledge acquisition methods may shape conceptual mastery in private institutions of learning in Uganda. It examines and brings together the conceptual and theoretical perspectives represented in the literature cited by different authors, including constructivist learning, deep approaches to learning, critical thinking, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, experiential learning, formative assessment, and technology-supported instruction. The review also looks at the advantages and disadvantages of artificial intelligence and digital knowledge-management tools. The reviewed literature consistently argues that conceptual mastery occurs when learners actively connect new material with prior knowledge, explain ideas, investigate problems, receive feedback, reflect on their learning, and transfer knowledge to authentic tasks. Lectures and other educators can provide all the necessary explanations and provide foundational knowledge, but they may not support mastery when they are used as the only instructional method or when majorly paired with recall-based examinations.
